- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly to align with mean reversion.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤ -0.67), model underestimates; adjust upward, especially if recent price is trending up.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >+5% from prior peak), model often overshoots; cap forecast at 1–2% below peak or use lagged 3–5 day average as ceiling.
- If model consistently forecasts higher than true outcome over 3–5 days, apply downward bias correction (e.g., subtract 0.5–1.5% per day from forecast).
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.33–0.67), model often misses mean reversion; use 3–7 day moving average or 10-day smoothed trend as anchor.
- For 30-day horizon, avoid overreacting to single-day sentiment spikes; use sentiment average over last 5–7 days as weighting factor for correction.
- If true outcome is consistently lower than forecast, especially after a spike, apply “lag correction” — delay forecast by 1–2 days or reduce slope of upward trend.
- If sentiment turns negative after a positive spike, model often fails to adjust; force downward correction by 1–3% if sentiment drops below 0.33.
